title: Hermes Consultant Intermediate: Practice Exam
description: Timed practice exam covering the whole series. Pass with 72% or higher to earn the course completion certificate.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
The 30-45 minute task is the unit of execution.
The 30-45 minute task is not the unit of execution.
The lesson recommends treating output as final without review.
questions.explanation: The 30-45 minute task is the unit of execution.

questions.question: Per the lesson about managing a small portfolio of clients, what is the central focus?
options: Keeping several engagements alive and honest by defending scope, holding expectations, and allocating time across the whole set
A history of client management software
A review of unrelated calendar tools
A summary of finance policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a portfolio is several commitments sharing one brain, and the craft is naming, measuring, and controlling the three enemies.

questions.question: Per the lesson about change management as a deliverable, what is the central focus?
options: Treating change to a live delivery as its own deliverable with scope, risk, test, rollback, and record, not a drive-by edit
A history of version control
A review of unrelated config tools
A summary of procurement policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a live delivery drifts one small unrecorded edit at a time unless change is treated as a bounded, visible deliverable.

questions.question: Per the lesson about incident discipline, what is the central focus?
options: A history of incident management software
A review of unrelated debugging tools
Diagnosing a broken agent methodically under client pressure, by establishing ground truth, diagnosing before patching, and verifying a fix
A summary of HR policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the discipline that kills the rush to patch and keeps a live failure from becoming a crisis.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Running a Full Engagement”, what is the central focus?
options: Turning the five-phase lifecycle into a week-by-week plan: mapping discover, design, implement, handover, and support onto a real calendar, with gates, buffers, and the scheduling realities that kill engagements.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: Turning the five-phase lifecycle into a week-by-week plan: mapping discover, design, implement, handover, and support onto a real calendar, with gates, buffers, and the scheduling realities that kill engagements.

questions.question: Per the lesson about team delivery, what is the central focus?
options: A history of collaboration software
Splitting work across owners on the axes of who owns it and in what order, with the seam as a written durable contract
A review of unrelated project tools
A summary of HR policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that splitting work is interface design, and nearly every team that fails is failing at a seam, not a part.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: A scope that says deliver an agent that improves the support workflow is a strong boundary
An acceptance criterion is a test, not a description, so the agent clears ninety percent of the golden set is better than it should be accurate
Name only what you will do, and leave the out-of-scope list out
Keep the price assumptions silent so you are not pinned down
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that an acceptance criterion is a test you can run and count, and an out-of-scope list is a fence that protects the fixed-fee.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Set the conversion gate after the pilot succeeds so the client has seen the proof
The conversion gate is set before the pilot starts, with the scope, price, and timeline sketched in advance
A baseline can be estimated after the pilot from memory
Price the engagement from a market guess rather than the pilot's evidence
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that after the pilot the power shifts, so the gate with its terms must be agreed before it proves anything.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The rollback plan is improvised after the change lands
The rollback is the most important artifact and must be written before the change, specific to the exact prior state
A change to a system that runs itself needs no gates because nobody is watching anyway
Tell the client about a high-risk change after it lands since the output looks the same
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a change that cannot be rolled back cleanly is a change you cannot afford to be wrong about, so the revert is written before the change.

questions.question: Per the lesson about the internal pilot, what is the central focus?
options: Scoping a real slice of a prospect's problem as a bounded proof that converts into a signed engagement instead of a free spec
A history of sales enablement
A review of unrelated demo tools
A summary of pricing policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the craft of the fence that keeps a pilot from becoming a free engagement and turns it into a transaction.

questions.question: Per the lesson about working with IT, compliance, and legal, what is the central focus?
options: A history of corporate governance
A review of unrelated legal tools
Treating a rollout as a stakeholder channel, triaging the three teams in early, and planning it backward from the go-live date
A summary of sales policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the rollout lives in other people's workflows and is a stakeholder channel to plan, not a hurdle to clear at the end.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A handover is written on the last day so it describes the final system
Measurement is defined after the change so it fits the result
Design for a loud failure that stops rather than producing plausible output from unexpected input
The golden set is graded by the delivered system itself
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the most valuable build decision is that the pipeline stops rather than produces plausible output, so failures are loud and diagnosable.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: A drive-by edit feels small because nothing breaks visibly, so it needs no record
Bundling extra unrequested edits into an approved change is efficient and harmless
Scope the change like a mini-engagement: what changes, what does not, who approves, and how to roll back
Trust your own judgment over a test because you built the original
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that each meaningful change answers the same questions as the original build in miniature, turning a drive-by edit into a visible deliverable.

questions.question: Per the lesson about measuring outcomes and reporting value to the buyer, what is the central focus?
options: Measuring the activity an agent generates, such as sessions, tokens, and run counts
Proving delivery by pointing at a working, stable agent system
Measuring outcomes rather than activity, against a pre-agreed baseline, and reporting value in the buyer's language
Delivering a single large value report at the end of the engagement
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that delivery (you built what you said) is not value (the buyer is better off), so the consultant measures business outcomes against a frozen baseline and reports them in the buyer's units.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The opposite is true: lesson 4 gave you the toolkit: packaged, trigger-first skills that let the next engagement start from a running start instead of a blank page.
Lesson 4 gave you the toolkit: packaged, trigger-first skills that let the next engagement start from a running start instead of a blank page.
The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
The lesson recommends treating output as final without review.
questions.explanation: Lesson 4 gave you the toolkit: packaged, trigger-first skills that let the next engagement start from a running start instead of a blank page.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Spread each client's work thinly across the week to stay responsive
Let the loudest client extract whatever time they need that week
The weekly portfolio review forces the whole set into view so a quiet client does not quietly starve
Deliver every routine report by hand to keep quality high
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the engagement in front of you always demands attention, so a fixed weekly review catches the client you are not looking at.

questions.question: Per the lesson about writing proposals and statements of work, what is the central focus?
options: A history of contract law
A review of unrelated document tools
A summary of accounting policy
Writing the proposal and SOW as risk documents with a specific scope boundary, testable acceptance criteria, and written exclusions and change control
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the only protection that works in a dispute is specificity, and templates are specifically vague.

questions.question: Per the lesson about pricing engagements, what is the central focus?
options: Choosing between fixed-fee and time-and-materials by allocating estimation risk, priced from a real unit economy and defended with change control
A history of consulting fees
A review of unrelated billing tools
A summary of accounting policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the price is a risk allocation you choose, not a number you pick, and the contract mechanism decides who carries the uncertainty.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Never version a framework because it is the final method
A framework without gates is a timeline, and the gate is where a failure becomes cheap and visible
Automate a step before the process is stable to save time
The v1 should be the perfect system built on your first pass
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the gate discipline is what makes delivery repeatable and priceable, and that v1 is the honest first cut.

questions.question: Per the lesson about vendor-agnostic translation, what is the central focus?
options: Separating the transferable discipline from the tool-specific mechanics so the playbook works on whatever agent a client runs
A history of agent vendors
A review of unrelated integration tools
A summary of procurement policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that your expertise is the playbook, not the tool, and the discipline transfers while the mechanics do not.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: The golden set is a document you write once and lock forever
Move the expected output to match the system when a case fails, to keep the gate green
The golden set is living reference data with provenance, grown with restraint, and never edited to encode today's bug
A case with provenance is a guess that will eventually be removed
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the set exists to hold the bar, so you never move the expected output just to make the gate pass.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The lesson states this is never a relevant consideration.
Level 1 gave you the container: five phases, discover, design, implement, handover, support, each with a product and an exit test.
The lesson says the opposite: this should always be avoided.
The opposite is true: level 1 gave you the container: five phases, discover, design, implement, handover, support, each with a product and an exit test.
questions.explanation: Level 1 gave you the container: five phases, discover, design, implement, handover, support, each with a product and an exit test.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Absorb the duplicate-SKU cleanup into the engagement because you are in the data anyway
Name a client defect with evidence and refuse to own it, pricing around it instead of absorbing it
Keep silent to the sponsor about the Tuesday the export changed
Decline the follow-on order entry work without explaining why
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that rolling the cleanup in would cost unpaid days, make exclusions soft, and hide a data governance problem, so you name the defect and refuse to own it.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Review is a bottleneck, and it is almost never where you think.
The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
The lesson says the opposite: this should always be avoided.
Review is not a bottleneck, and it is almost never where you think.
questions.explanation: Review is a bottleneck, and it is almost never where you think.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Building a Reusable Delivery Toolkit: Skill Packaging Done Right”, what is the central focus?
options: The difference between a consultant who solves one client's problem and one who compounds every engagement into the next: turning the working capture discipline, eval suite, and guardrail set from Lessons 2 and 3 into packaged, loadable skills another consultant can run without relearning them.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The difference between a consultant who solves one client's problem and one who compounds every engagement into the next: turning the working capture discipline, eval suite, and guardrail set from Lessons 2 and 3 into packaged, loadable skills another consultant can run without relearning them.

questions.question: Per the lesson about handover that makes the client self-sufficient, what is the central focus?
options: Transferring ownership so the client can run, change, and recover the system, with operating docs, runbooks, a dry run, and a taper
A history of documentation tools
A review of unrelated wiki software
A summary of IT policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the deliverable is the agent plus the knowledge of how to operate it, transferred so your presence becomes optional.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Lesson 2 taught you to capture requirements as-built, with the rule, the exception, and the boundary written down so they survive handover.
The lesson says the opposite: this should always be avoided.
The opposite is true: lesson 2 taught you to capture requirements as-built, with the rule, the exception, and the boundary written down so they survive handover.
The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 taught you to capture requirements as-built, with the rule, the exception, and the boundary written down so they survive handover.

questions.question: Per the lesson about building repeatable processes, what is the central focus?
options: A history of process management
A review of unrelated documentation tools
A summary of HR policy
Building checklists, decision-history templates, and a versioned delivery framework extracted from the engagements you actually ran
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches how a practice stops depending on one person remembering everything by building and versioning repeatable assets.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Answer compliance with assurances that the system is fine
Secrets can live in a prompt as long as they are needed for the task
Least privilege gives each agent the narrowest set of credentials the task requires, and compliance is answered with evidence, not claims
One approval mode can be a blanket across interactive and unattended work
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that secrets are scoped to the narrowest task and compliance is satisfied by legible records and documentation, not assurances.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Under pressure, change something quickly and claim it is fixed
A fix is a conclusion, not a first action: diagnose first, then patch, then verify
A confident wrong explanation sounds better than admitting you do not know
Assume the software is the cause so you debug the code first
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that skipping diagnosis means guessing, and a patch on top of a wrong diagnosis entangles the failure.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Design the framework from a textbook so it is complete and correct
A checklist is a to-do list that restates the work you already planned
A checklist names the silent, expensive step that has actually failed, and a template field carries the reasoning a past engagement learned
Build the framework as the final version so it never changes
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a checklist is a pre-mortem device and a template is a captured decision history, each designed against a real failure.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance on when and how to capture a baseline?
options: Reconstruct the baseline after delivery from the client's memory of the old process
Freeze the baseline in writing, from the client's real data, before the solution exists, so neither side can drift the before-state
Offer a baseline estimate to the client and let them correct it at the end
Use token and session counts as the baseline since they are easy to collect
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a baseline reconstructed later gets idealized in memory, so the honest consultant records the agreed, data-backed starting number before the solution exists.

questions.question: Per the lesson about managing scope creep and difficult clients, what is the central focus?
options: Settling scope creep and difficult clients with a written scope, a named acceptance bar, and a change process
A review of negotiation tactics
A history of client management
A summary of HR policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that creep and difficult clients are one problem, the engagement drifting from its baseline, fixed by three structural artifacts.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
The lesson advises ignoring this entirely in practice.
The opposite is true: lesson 3 taught you to harden a single agent for production: route its work by tier, prove its output against a gold set, and hold its boundaries by construction.
Lesson 3 taught you to harden a single agent for production: route its work by tier, prove its output against a gold set, and hold its boundaries by construction.
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 taught you to harden a single agent for production: route its work by tier, prove its output against a gold set, and hold its boundaries by construction.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: A pilot is a chance to show off what the tool can do and impress the client
The pilot must prove the whole engagement so the client sees it all work
The pilot is a hypothesis test with a specific, measurable, falsifiable claim written before you build
Use clean synthetic data so the pilot always succeeds
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a pilot that converts is a hypothesis test, not a demo, and the claim names the deliverable, accuracy, time, and cost.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Report every metric you can measure so the buyer sees the full picture
Ignore alternative explanations so the agent appears to own all the improvement
Report on your own convenience and deliver the full story in the closing meeting
Name the counterfactual yourself, claim only the share the agent honestly owns, and report on the buyer's rhythm in small honest installments
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that three airtight metrics beat eight with a soft link, that naming the other initiative first preserves credibility, and that repeated small reports build trust better than a single end-of-engagement reveal.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
The existing stack is not not an obstacle to work around.
The existing stack is not an obstacle to work around.
The lesson claims this cannot be verified at all.
questions.explanation: The existing stack is not an obstacle to work around.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Complex Client Environments: Existing Stacks, Enterprise Constraints, and Sandboxed Deploys”, what is the central focus?
options: The clean single-client world where you chose the stack is the exception, not the rule. This lesson teaches you to land a packaged agent delivery inside a company that already has infrastructure, security rules, and processes you did not choose, and to keep the toolkit working when the environment fights back.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The clean single-client world where you chose the stack is the exception, not the rule. This lesson teaches you to land a packaged agent delivery inside a company that already has infrastructure, security rules, and processes you did not choose, and to keep the toolkit working when the environment fights back.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Fixed-fee is the right call when you do not know the work, because it gives the client certainty
Time-and-materials is the right call when the scope is understood and the environment is known
Fixed-fee is right when you genuinely know the work, and T&M is honest when you cannot name the deliverable
The client should always hold the estimation risk because they have deeper pockets
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that fixed-fee is for known work and T&M for exploratory work, with the risk sitting on the side that can best manage it.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Status reflects a hopeful prediction of when the system will recover
A confident recovery time builds more trust than a humble honest one
Write the failure mode down only after the incident when details are calm
Report what you know, label what you do not, and commit to a cadence of honest updates rather than one invented timeline
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a confident wrong timeline destroys more trust than a humble correct one, so you commit to a stream of honest updates.

questions.question: Per the lesson about cost and reliability engineering for an agent estate, what is the central focus?
options: Modeling and containing recurring spend of a fleet of agents while engineering so no single part takes the whole delivery down
A history of cloud billing
A review of unrelated monitoring tools
A summary of sales policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a running estate is a recurring cost plus a standing reliability obligation, and the levers are shared.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Advanced Hermes Configuration: Model Routing, Evals, and Guardrails in Production”, what is the central focus?
options: When the agent leaves the sandbox and runs at real volume in front of a client, three decisions decide whether it holds up: which model runs which task, how you prove the output is still correct, and how you keep the guardrails you documented actually enforced.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: When the agent leaves the sandbox and runs at real volume in front of a client, three decisions decide whether it holds up: which model runs which task, how you prove the output is still correct, and how you keep the guardrails you documented actually enforced. This lesson teaches all three.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Scope creep in one engagement is harmless because it is extra work
One client per profile makes the scope boundary an architectural fact rather than a mental reminder
Promising an hour response time to every client is the honest move
Run committed hours at one hundred percent of capacity to maximize output
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a profile isolates each client's config, memory, skills, and jobs, so scope separation is enforced by the platform.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: File handover, producing the artifacts, is the whole job
The operating doc is reference and the runbook is procedure, and the two answer different questions
Write the runbook for the engineer who built the thing
A document you wrote is proven once it is written
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the operating doc answers how the system is configured while the runbook tells a stranger what to do when something breaks.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Copy the Hermes artifact into the new tool's format and the discipline follows
Force the new tool to be Hermes by building fake structures for concepts it never had
Map each intent to the primitive that genuinely carries it, then verify the behavior held in the new tool
Memorize the exact config syntax of every agent tool because it is the valuable layer
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the three-layer model: intent, mapping, and implementation, and to map each intent to a real primitive and verify it holds.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: IT, compliance, and legal are a single obstacle to plan against as one
Build the agent first and ask how long the rollout will take after
Present the same demonstration deck to every team
Start the sticky gates, legal review, procurement, IT provisioning, in parallel with the build so the channel is open when the agent is ready
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches backward planning: the slowest gate is the schedule, so sticky gates start in week one while the build runs.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: The weekly burn is estimated after handover so the client sees a settled number
Route the mechanical share of the fleet off the model entirely, into no-agent scripts that cost nothing and cannot drift
Run every judgment job on the most capable model at full reasoning effort for consistency
Give every job a full fallback chain regardless of how trivial the run is
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the cheapest reliable run never calls a model, so deterministic mechanical work belongs in no-agent scripts.

questions.question: Per the lesson about the real agent engagement case study, what is the central focus?
options: One agent engagement from first call to handover, told in sequence with the mistakes left in, to teach sequencing over techniques
A review of unrelated sales tools
A history of the ERP vendor
A summary of procurement policy
questions.explanation: The lesson runs twenty techniques together in sequence because the sequence is the part no single technique lesson can teach.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The lesson says the opposite: this should always be avoided.
The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
An integration delay pushes everything after it, and the pessimistic case of an early task becomes the starting condition of the next.
The opposite is true: an integration delay pushes everything after it, and the pessimistic case of an early task becomes the starting condition of the next.
questions.explanation: An integration delay pushes everything after it, and the pessimistic case of an early task becomes the starting condition of the next.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A translation worked when the files are in place in the new format
An honest capability gap is a deliverable with a price and a sign-off, not something to paper over
If a tool has no primitive for an intent, improvise a fragile approximation and call it done
A behavioral instruction is a structural guardrail as long as it is written well
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that when a tool cannot hold an intent, you name the gap with its price and options rather than trusting it will be fine.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Requirement Capture as an As-Built Discipline”, what is the central focus?
options: Moving from a problem statement you agree on to a requirement set that survives handover: capturing the enacted process, not the stated one, and writing requirements the next team can run and change without you.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: Moving from a problem statement you agree on to a requirement set that survives handover: capturing the enacted process, not the stated one, and writing requirements the next team can run and change without you.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Estimating Multi-Week Engagements: Beyond the 30-45 Minute Task”, what is the central focus?
options: The 30-45 minute task is the unit of execution, not the unit of estimation.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The 30-45 minute task is the unit of execution, not the unit of estimation. This lesson teaches you to size a real multi-week delivery: how to break a large engagement into estimable pieces, why you estimate the critical path and not the total, how to put the constraints and reviews from Lesson 5 into the number, and how to keep an estimate honest when the environment reveals surprises.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A failing gate with no owner is fine because the deploy deadline is real
A red gate is triaged as a real regression, stale reference, or flaky test, each with a different fix
High false alarms are harmless because the gate still protects
A gate that fires and is ignored is better than no gate because it creates awareness
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a failing gate is an event with an owner, and naming which of the three diagnoses it is is the whole skill.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Change control is a scope skill separate from pricing
A fixed-fee with no enforced change control quietly becomes time-and-materials where you forgot to charge the time
Every addition to a fixed-fee engagement is absorbed into the margin to keep the client happy
A T&M engagement needs no budget guardrail because the client chose it
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the price is only as stable as the change control that defends it, so a fixed-fee must enforce its boundary.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The handover is real when you narrate the demo to the client
Secrets belong in the operating doc so the operator knows the values
The dry run has an unbriefed operator recover a deliberately failed run using only the runbook while you stay silent
Leave on a single day so the client owns it immediately
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the handover passes when an unbriefed stranger can run the recovery procedure to a successful end while you say nothing.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Lesson 1 gave you the calendar: five phases mapped onto real weeks, with gates and buffers and a decision rule for slippage.
The lesson recommends treating output as final without review.
The opposite is true: lesson 1 gave you the calendar: five phases mapped onto real weeks, with gates and buffers and a decision rule for slippage.
The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 gave you the calendar: five phases mapped onto real weeks, with gates and buffers and a decision rule for slippage.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: When an unpinned job's global default changes, the job should silently inherit the switch so the fleet stays running
A broken job may fail quietly since a fleet has redundancy
A misconfigured job should burn tokens to prove it is broken
An unattended job should fail closed and alert rather than guess and spend, so cost control and reliability are the same mechanism
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the fails-closed posture: an unpinned job whose default changes skips, alerts, and spends no inference, protecting both budget and honesty.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: You pick it, then you prove it, then you revisit it when the output drifts.
The lesson advises ignoring this entirely in practice.
The lesson recommends treating output as final without review.
The opposite is true: you pick it, then you prove it, then you revisit it when the output drifts.
questions.explanation: You pick it, then you prove it, then you revisit it when the output drifts.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Compliance wants a feature demo and IT wants your enthusiasm
To IT present the agent as a component that must operate safely, to compliance as a demonstrable process, and to legal as contractually bounded scope
Write the statement of work about the agent you are building, not the deliverable
A rollout ends at go-live the day the agent starts
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the same decision is translated into each team's language, and each team gets the artifact it acts on.

questions.question: Per the lesson about quality at scale, what is the central focus?
options: Keeping output correct at volume with a living golden set, binding eval gates, and regression discipline that triages failures
A history of QA software
A review of unrelated testing tools
A summary of compliance policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that volume defeats review, so you gate changes and sample the live stream instead of reading everything.
